output.title: Customer-facing web app returning 5xx errors
output.symptoms: A customer-facing application, such as the Customer Portal, returns 500/502/503 errors, or synthetic monitors fail.
output.cause: A bad deployment, exhausted connection pools, failing downstream dependencies, or autoscaling reaching its maximum instance count during a traffic spike.
steps: Check the deployment history. If a release happened within the last 24 hours, consider rolling back first.
Review application logs and APM traces for the failing endpoint.
Check instance counts against autoscaling limits, and check database connection pool metrics.
If instances are at the autoscaling maximum, raise the max instance limit.
Add a CPU-based scaling policy so the app scales out before traffic spikes exhaust capacity.
Post customer communication through the status page if the outage lasts more than 15 minutes.
output.rationale: KB0010026 already names autoscaling limits as a cause but only says to check them, so it is updated with the fix of raising the max instance limit and adding a CPU-based scaling policy.
KB0010025 already covers stale reporting data from replica replication lag caused by IO saturation, including pausing maintenance jobs, which is exactly how this incident was resolved.

KB0010024 already covers report query timeouts caused by a missing index as tables grow, including checking missing index recommendations and table growth and creating a change request for new indexes, which matches this fix.
KB0010023 already covers a blocked invoice caused by a closed posting period and the fix of confirming with finance and opening the period in OB52, which is how this incident was resolved.

KB0010021 already documents month-end batch jobs competing with interactive users and the fix of rescheduling non-critical batch jobs and adding dialog work processes, which is exactly how this incident was resolved.
KB0010022 already covers a PO stuck in the SAP release workflow because of missing cost center master data, and the fix applied here was to correct the data and restart the workflow.
KB0010012 already lists a failing dock power supply as a cause and dock replacement as the fix, which is exactly how this incident was resolved.

KB0010011 already covers BitLocker recovery prompts and blue screens at boot caused by motherboard failure, including vendor diagnostics, a loaner, a vendor warranty case and restoring data from OneDrive.

KB0010010 already lists low disk space from the OneDrive cache as a cause of slow startup and a constantly running fan, and its step to enable Files On-Demand and clear temp files is exactly how this incident was fixed.

KB0010032 already covers MDM enrollment failure caused by an OS version below the compliance policy, and its steps (check compliance reason, update OS, re-check status) match the fix used, even though the close notes inconsistently mention iOS for an Android phone.

notes: evidence=strong: The surge was caused by a vendor-side Exchange Online service incident that affected mail flow, tracked as major incident MI20260120-email. Confidence is high:

output.title: Exchange Online service incident disrupted mail flow across all Meridian sites (week of 2026-01-19)
output.problem_statement: In the week of 2026-01-19, users at all six sites (Atlanta DC, Chicago HQ, Dallas DC, Memphis DC, Remote, Toronto Office) raised email tickets about Outlook not receiving mail, not syncing, stuck on 'Updating' or disconnected. Volume reached 150 tickets against a baseline of 7.75 a week, about 142 above baseline, consuming 680.8 resolution hours with 1 SLA breach.
output.root_cause_hypothesis: The surge was caused by a vendor-side Exchange Online service incident that affected mail flow, tracked as major incident MI20260120-email. Confidence is high: that fix resolved 95% of surge tickets against 33% of this subcategory's tickets outside surges, and volume returned to baseline (5 tickets) the following week. The open questions are not the cause itself but Meridian's exposure to it: the absence of early detection and of mass-communication or ticket-deduplication when a vendor outage hits.
evidence: 150 email tickets in the week of 2026-01-19 versus a 7.75/week baseline (about 142 above baseline); the surrounding weeks ranged from 5 to 12.
The Exchange Online service incident fix resolved 95% of surge tickets, compared with 33% of this subcategory's tickets outside surges.
680.8 resolution hours were spent, with 1 SLA breach; the sampled incident-linked tickets each took 3.1-6.8 h, apparently waiting on vendor mitigation.
Tickets came from all 6 sites, including Remote, consistent with a cloud-service outage rather than a local network or site issue.
output.workaround: The service desk linked each ticket to the parent incident and waited for the vendor to mitigate Exchange Online, then confirmed mail flow was restored; several tickets also followed KB0010015. Isolated non-outage cases, such as a corrupted OST file, were resolved by rebuilding the Outlook profile and resyncing the mailbox.
output.permanent_fix: The outage itself is vendor-controlled, so Meridian cannot prevent it directly. The permanent fix is to reduce its impact: add proactive Microsoft 365 Service Health monitoring with automated alerting to Messaging & Collaboration. Pair it with a predefined mass-communication and ticket-deduplication process, such as a service desk banner/IVR message and auto-linking to the parent incident. This would stop the flood of individual tickets and the resolution hours spent on each.
next_steps: Review major incident MI20260120-email, including the vendor's post-incident report, and confirm the timeline and Meridian's detection-to-communication lag.
Raise a change request to configure Microsoft 365 Service Health alerts (API or webhook) to page Messaging & Collaboration and trigger the major-incident process automatically.
Update KB0010015 (or create a companion KB) with a vendor-outage triage path: check Service Health first, link to the parent incident, and avoid OST/profile rebuilds during known outages.
Establish a service desk template for outage banners and user notifications to deflect duplicate tickets during future Exchange Online incidents.

output.title: GlobalProtect client upgrade leaves remote users with a corrupted cached portal configuration
output.problem_statement: Since the week of 2026-05-04, remote users have repeatedly been unable to connect to VPN after their GlobalProtect client moved to the new version with a corrupted portal configuration. The surge lasted 6 weeks to the week of 2026-06-08 and produced 135 tickets, about 100 above the 5.83/week baseline, consuming 1088 resolution hours with 6 SLA breaches.
output.root_cause_hypothesis: The rollout of the new GlobalProtect client version most likely corrupts or fails to migrate the cached portal settings on remote endpoints, so the client cannot reach or authenticate to the portal. Confidence is high. The same fix (clear cached portal settings and re-enter the portal address) resolved 100% of surge tickets, against 34% of this subcategory's tickets outside surges. The surge began abruptly at 23 tickets in the week of 2026-05-04, up from 2 the week before. The exact upgrade mechanism (deployment package, default config, or portal-side change) is not confirmed by the data.
evidence: Weekly volume jumped from 2 (week of 2026-04-27) to 23 (week of 2026-05-04) and stayed at 19-25 for 6 weeks, versus a 5.83/week baseline.
The dominant fix resolved 100% of the 135 surge tickets, compared with 34% of this subcategory's tickets outside surges.
Impact was 1088 resolution hours and 6 SLA breaches; sample ticket resolution times ranged from 0.7 h to 19.4 h.

output.title: Recurring WAN/web slowness across sites from degraded proxy pool nodes and business-hours backup jobs saturating WAN circuits
output.problem_statement: From the week of 2026-07-06 through the week of 2026-07-20, Network Operations received 18 WAN slowness tickets ('internet very slow', 'websites taking forever to load') across Atlanta DC, Chicago HQ, Dallas DC, Memphis DC and Toronto Office, about 13 above the 1.75-per-week baseline. These tickets consumed 268.8 resolution hours with no SLA breaches.
output.root_cause_hypothesis: Confidence is low. No single cause clearly explains the surge. The dominant fix was removing a degraded proxy node from the pool (KB0010009), but it resolved only 44% of surge tickets, below its 57% share outside surges. That points away from proxy degradation as the driver of the increase. In the samples, a second cause appears in the later surge weeks: large backup jobs running during business hours saturated the WAN circuits at Toronto Office and Dallas DC. Those backup jobs may account for much of the excess volume, while proxy node degradation looks like a chronic, recurring background issue that needs its own fix. The data does not establish whether the backup jobs were newly scheduled or changed in July.

The proxy-node fix resolved 44% of surge tickets versus 57% outside surges, so it explains proportionally fewer surge tickets than usual.
4 of 8 sample tickets (Toronto Office 2026-07-15 and 2026-07-22; Dallas DC 2026-07-21 and 2026-07-24) were resolved by rescheduling business-hours backup jobs that saturated the WAN circuit.

Update KB0010009 or create a companion KB covering diagnosis of backup-driven WAN saturation, to shorten resolution times that currently reach 30.2 h.

Confidence is high but not confirmed: the same fix resolved 100% of surge tickets versus 34% of this subcategory's tickets outside surges, and the surge began abruptly and subsided after mid-June, consistent with an upgrade wave. The upgrade mechanism (installer, pushed config, or portal-side change) still needs to be verified against deployment records.
